strengths: Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art execution accuracy on BIRD-dev (77.84%) and Spider-test (89.75%) with a 7B open model trained only on the BIRD training set, outperforming both fine-tuned open-source systems and closed-source pipelines (e.g., CHASE-SQL + Gemini at 74.90%).

Thorough ablation studies: component-level ablations (Table 3), max interaction turns during RL (Table 10 / Figure 3), Best-of-N scaling (Table 11), and selection-strategy comparisons (Table 14) collectively support the design claims.

The Validation Agent is shown to meaningfully outperform reasonable alternatives (Self-Consistency, GPT-4.1 LLM-as-Judge) on the same candidate pool, isolating the value of the learned verifier rather than just more sampling.

Good transparency: full prompts (Tables 7, 9, 12, 13), training hyperparameters (Tables 4-6), dataset construction details (Appendix C), and a reproducibility statement; the grounding agent's recall/precision analysis (Table 8) adds useful diagnostic detail.
Clean out-of-domain story: strong Spider/Spider-DK performance without training on Spider data, contrasted explicitly with competitors that trained on Spider-derived data.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the framework is a combination of established techniques (GRPO, ReAct-style multi-turn interaction, generative verifiers from Zhang et al. 2025b) applied to Text-to-SQL. The claim that 'explicit RL for this domain remains underexplored' is questionable given SkyRL-SQL (Liu et al., 2025a), which performs multi-turn RL for Text-to-SQL and whose framework the authors themselves adapt - yet SkyRL-SQL is absent from the baseline comparison, which is a significant omission.

Unfair compute comparison: MARS-SQL reports results using 8 rollouts plus a verifier (and M stochastic verification rounds), while many baselines are single-pass systems. No compute-matched comparison (e.g., baselines with 8 samples + selection) is provided, and inference cost is not analyzed, making the headline SOTA claim harder to interpret.

Circularity in Validation Agent training: the verifier's training data is generated by the trained Generation Agent itself, and for questions with only flawed trajectories, ground-truth SQL is injected into prompts as hints - this may leak oracle information into the verifier and is not analyzed for its impact.

Evidence-quality gaps: no variance or statistical significance reporting (single-run results for RL training), and the claimed 'synergistic effect' (full model gain far exceeding the sum of component contributions) is asserted rather than demonstrated - Table 3 actually shows 'w/o Grounder' nearly matches full Spider-test performance (89.19 vs 89.75), which weakens the claim that each agent is indispensable.

Inference configuration for the main results (Table 2) is underspecified: which T, N, and verification settings produce the headline numbers is not clearly stated, hurting reproducibility and comparability.

Presentation issues: Figure 5 and Figure 1 show the interaction rounds out of chronological order (round 2's thought precedes round 1's error correction), typos throughout ('taui', 'Obeservation', 'Unkonwn'), and the code link in the abstract is empty - code is only promised 'upon publication'.
No dedicated limitations discussion (e.g., dependence on BIRD's data distribution, verifier failure modes when all candidates are wrong, cost of M stochastic verification rounds).

strengths: Strong empirical results: the framework achieves competitive execution accuracy (77.84% on BIRD-dev, 89.75% on Spider-test) with a 7B model trained only on BIRD, and the out-of-domain generalization claim (no Spider training data) is well-motivated.

The core component studies are reasonably thorough: the interaction-turn ablation (Table 10) is informative, showing that training with more turns narrows the greedy vs. best-of-n gap; the grounding recall/precision analysis (Table 8) and best-of-N scaling analysis (Table 11) add useful detail.
The selection-method comparison (Table 14) against self-consistency and LLM-as-a-judge baselines supports the claim that a fine-tuned generative verifier outperforms generic selection strategies.
Reproducibility artifacts are partially strong: hyperparameters for all three training stages are provided, prompts are included in the appendix, and the datasets/metric are standard.
The paper is generally well organized, and the formalization of Text-to-SQL as a multi-turn decision process is clearly stated.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The framework is an assembly of established components: GRPO (DeepSeekMath), ReAct-style Think-Act-Observe loops, generative verifiers (Zhang et al., 2025b), and the SkyRL/Verl training infrastructure. Multi-turn RL with execution rewards for Text-to-SQL already exists (SkyRL-SQL, Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, Reasoning-SQL); the main delta is a fine-tuned verifier grafted onto a pipeline. Notably, SkyRL-SQL — the framework the paper itself adapts — is cited but absent from the main comparison table, which weakens the SOTA claim.

Table 1 is a misleading strawman: it claims open-source and closed-source systems lack 'Interactive Reasoning' and 'Efficient Selection', but closed-source systems like CHASE-SQL and XiYan-SQL explicitly use candidate generation and selection, and several use iterative execution feedback. No evidence or citation substantiates these ✗ marks.

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers: Table 3's 'w/o verifier' configuration (Grounding + RL Generator, 68.71% BIRD-dev) is hard to reconcile with Table 10, where the same generator with grounding reaches ~77% 'Selected' accuracy; Table 10's best Selected score (77.57%) also does not match the headline 77.84% without explanation of the differing configuration. Figure 5's round ordering is scrambled (the 'I made a mistake in the table name' thought appears after the observation it is responding to), and the narrative in Appendix E does not match the figure.

The SOTA claim on Spider-test rests on a 0.10-point margin over XiYan-SQL (89.75% vs 89.65%), with no significance testing, no variance over seeds, and no evidence of official leaderboard submission for the Spider test set (whose labels are not public) — the evaluation protocol for the test set is not described.

Key experimental details are missing or unclear: the number of inference rollouts N used for headline results is never stated in the main text; the validation score 'averaged across M stochastic reasoning rounds' is undefined (the verifier outputs a single Yes/No token — what is sampled M times?); the computational cost of best-of-8 plus per-candidate verification is not reported despite claims of 'Efficient Selection'.

The claimed reward design has errors/oddities: in the Grounding reward, max(0.5, |Cg|/|Cp|) is redundant since |Cg|/|Cp| ≤ 1 for a superset; the reward table formatting conflates cases; small typos pervade the paper ('Obeservation', 'taui', 'baesd', 'Unkonwn', 'MARS-SQLsecures'), suggesting insufficient care.

No limitations section. The paper motivates the work via real-world enterprise databases (Spider 2.0) but evaluates only on academic benchmarks; there is no discussion of this gap, of benchmark contamination risk for a BIRD-trained verifier applied to Spider-DK, or of inference cost.

The 'synergistic effect' claim in Section 4.3.1 is rhetorically inflated: w/o Grounder achieves 89.19% on Spider test vs. 89.75% full, so the grounding agent contributes marginally on two of three benchmarks, contradicting the framing that every agent is 'indispensable'.

strengths: Strong empirical results: 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test with a 7B open-source model, reportedly surpassing both trained open-source competitors (Reasoning-SQL 72.29%) and closed-source pipelines (CHASE-SQL + Gemini 74.90%) on BIRD-dev, with competitive OOD generalization on Spider-DK without Spider training data.

Comprehensive ablation studies covering each agent (Grounding, Verifier, Generator), training vs. inference interaction turns (Table 10), Best-of-N scaling (Table 11), and selection strategies vs. Self-Consistency and LLM-as-a-Judge baselines (Table 14), which support the claim that the full pipeline matters.

Good methodological transparency: GRPO objectives for both agents, explicit reward design with partial credit for grounding, full training data construction details (filtered BIRD, 16 candidate trajectories per question, best/worst-of-N curation), and complete prompts and hyperparameters in the appendix.
Reproducibility and ethics statements are present and reasonable; grounding agent is evaluated separately (recall/precision in Table 8), giving insight beyond the end-to-end metric.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over closely related prior work. The paper builds directly on SkyRL-SQL (multi-turn RL for Text-to-SQL), GRPO (DeepSeekMath), ReAct, and Generative Verifiers (Zhang et al., 2024), and the claim that 'explicit RL for this domain remains underexplored' contradicts its own cited baselines (Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, Reasoning-SQL, SkyRL-SQL). Critically, SkyRL-SQL—the framework the Generation Agent is explicitly adapted from—is absent from the main comparison table (Table 2), making it hard to isolate the contribution of MARS-SQL over its closest predecessor.

Comparison fairness is questionable. MARS-SQL's headline numbers use test-time scaling (N=8 rollouts plus ~5 stochastic verifier calls per candidate), while many baselines are single-pass; the inference compute per system is never quantified. The baseline table also contains errors (e.g., GPT-5 labeled 'Thinking? = No'), and Table 1's qualitative 'feature comparison' makes sweeping, unsupported claims (e.g., that no open-source system supports interactive reasoning) that read as marketing rather than analysis.

Some empirical claims are weakly supported or inconsistent. The 'synergistic effect' claim is partly undermined by Table 3, where removing the Grounder costs only ~0.6% on Spider-test (89.19 vs. 89.75). Table 10 reports Selected accuracy of 77.57 for the T=10 model with grounding, which does not match the 77.84 headline number; the discrepancy is not explained. The Spider-test result (89.75%) does not indicate whether official leaderboard evaluation was used, and potential benchmark contamination between BIRD training data and Spider evaluation is not discussed.

The Validation Agent introduces a circularity risk: it is SFT-trained on trajectories generated by the same Generator being evaluated, and its '97.15% correct selection rate' on Spider-test is reported without clarifying the candidate distribution or how ties/errors were handled, making the verifier analysis hard to interpret independently.

Presentation issues reduce polish: Figure 1/5 example rounds are presented out of chronological order (the 'no such table: fprm' observation precedes the corresponding thought), there are typos ('taui', 'Obeservation', 'baesd', 'Unkonwn'), the code URL in the abstract is empty, and the paper lacks a dedicated limitations section discussing compute cost and failure modes of multi-rollout inference.

strengths: Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art execution accuracy on BIRD-dev (77.84%) and Spider-test (89.75%) while training only on BIRD, with credible out-of-domain generalization (Spider-DK 78.13%, SParC 85.78%).

Unusually thorough and transparent efficiency analysis (Appendix F): end-to-end latency breakdown, token costs, VRAM under different deployment assumptions, tunable cost-accuracy operating points, and normalized-time-budget comparisons against self-consistency baselines, which directly addresses the 'gains come from extra compute' objection.

Well-designed causal attribution: the ablation suite (Table 2), controlled dataset-wide isolation starting from a strict RL-generator baseline (Table 3/23), parameter-matched ensemble comparison (Table 18), generator scaling to 14B (Table 19), and single-model multi-task baselines (Table 20) collectively show the gain comes from role-specialized interactive training rather than parameter count or best-of-N alone.

The controlled isolation result that the RL policy adds 44 correct queries under greedy decoding alone (Table 3) is a persuasive piece of evidence that execution-feedback interaction improves the underlying policy, not just selection.
Detailed reproducibility material: prompts, hyperparameters, training cost breakdown (~13 hours on 4xH800), dataset construction procedures, and a stated code release.
Honest treatment of the ~21B three-agent footprint as a limitation, including a candid discussion of the multi-agent specialization vs. single-model scaling trade-off.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the framework is an integration of established components (GRPO, ReAct-style Think-Act-Observe loops, multi-agent decomposition, generative verifiers from Zhang et al. 2025b). The 'first framework to leverage an interactive RL policy for tool-augmented SQL generation' claim in the conclusion is overstated given cited prior multi-turn RL text-to-SQL work (e.g., SkyRL-SQL, MtSQL-R1, Reasoning-SQL), which the paper itself acknowledges in Related Work.

Comparison fairness in Table 1: MARS-SQL uses 8 generation rollouts and 8 validation samples per query (~21B parameters), whereas many tabulated baselines are single-model/single-pass; the main paper defers this mostly to the appendix, and some closed-source baselines differ in model scale and API access, complicating the SOTA claim.

Citation irregularities raise concerns: references to 'GPT-5.2' (a model with no public existence), 'GPT-5 system card arXiv:2601.03267', and 'He et al., 2026, arXiv:2605.01357' are implausible or unverifiable; duplicate references appear (Wang et al. 2025a/2025b are the same MAC-SQL paper; ReAct cited as Yao 2022 and 2023), and typos ('detaile', 'baesd', 'MARS-SQLuses') suggest insufficient proofreading.

No variance/significance reporting: results appear to be single runs without seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, despite relatively small margins over some competitors on Spider-DK (78.13 vs. 81.5 actually being a loss to Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, which is correctly reported as second-best but trains on Spider data).

Validation Agent training has potential contamination-like issues: positive/negative pairs are curated from the generator's own trajectories, and gold SQL is injected into prompts for questions lacking correct trajectories, meaning the verifier's training signal partially depends on ground-truth access; the effect of this design choice is not ablated.

Grounding agent requires one inference call per table, which could be costly for very large enterprise schemas; the method's scalability beyond BIRD-scale schemas (54 columns/DB average) is not demonstrated (e.g., no Spider 2.0-style evaluation despite motivating enterprise complexity in the introduction).
Discussion of failure modes is thin: the paper reports Pass@8 upper bounds (83.76% on BIRD-dev) but offers limited analysis of which query categories the verifier still fails to recover.

strengths: Strong empirical results: reported state-of-the-art execution accuracy on BIRD-dev (77.84%) and Spider-test (89.75%), trained only on BIRD data, with out-of-domain evaluation on Spider-DK and SParC.

Unusually thorough ablation and attribution work: component ablations (Table 2), dataset-wide controlled isolation of each mechanism (Table 3/23), max-turn ablations (Table 24), best-of-N analysis (Table 25), grounding precision/recall (Table 27), and selection-strategy comparisons (Table 32).

Genuinely commendable effort to decouple gains from parameter count: comparisons against a parameter-matched ~21B ensemble (Table 18), a 14B-scaled generator (Table 19), and single-model multi-task baselines (Table 20).

Transparent efficiency reporting (latency, token cost, VRAM under different deployment assumptions, tunable cost-accuracy trade-offs in Appendix F), and an explicit, honest discussion of the ~21B inference footprint as a limitation.
Detailed training setup, prompts, hyperparameters, and qualitative case studies that make the framework reasonably reproducible in spirit.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the paper is an engineering combination of well-known components (GRPO, ReAct-style multi-turn interaction, multi-agent role decomposition, generative verifiers, test-time reranking). The claim of being 'the first framework to leverage an interactive RL policy for tool-augmented SQL generation' is overstated given closely related concurrent work the paper itself cites (SkyRL-SQL, MTSQL-R1, Reasoning-SQL, ExeSQL, Arctic-Text2SQL-R1), and the core contribution is a workflow/recipe rather than a new method.

Serious reference-integrity red flags: the bibliography contains apparently fabricated or impossible entries (e.g., 'He et al., 2026, arXiv:2605.01357' — an arXiv ID dated in the future; 'arXiv:2512.05671'; GPT-5 system card attributed to arXiv:2601.03267). The main text also evaluates a non-existent 'GPT-5.2' model (Tables 13-15). These errors undermine trust in the scholarship and suggest LLM-generated references were not verified.

Inconsistent numbers across the paper weaken confidence: e.g., the base model achieves 54.56 (Table 1), 66.37 (Table 2 'Generator Only (Base)'), and 54.43 (Table 24); the single-model multi-task baselines (55.67/57.82) are far below a simple generator-only baseline (66.37), suggesting the baseline configurations may be unfairly weak or mis-specified.

Potentially problematic data construction for the Validation Agent: when questions yield no correct trajectory, the ground-truth SQL is injected into the prompt as a 'suggestion' to generate proper trajectories, which risks leaking the answer into verifier training data and inflating verifier gains.

Speculative efficiency claims: the assertion that matching MARS-SQL with SFT would require '~15 million synthetic examples and 3-4 months' is based on a vague 'scaling laws' estimate with no supporting derivation; the SParC accuracy of 85.78% is unusually high for an untrained conversational benchmark and lacks verification detail.
No variance reporting, seeds, or statistical significance tests despite modest benchmark sizes (1,534 BIRD-dev examples); several gains (e.g., 68.71 vs 69.75 in Table 2) are within plausible noise.

Presentation quality is below standard: numerous typos ('detaile', 'taui', 'Unkonwn', 'MARS-SQLuses', 'baesd'), broken internal references ('Appendix 26'), and misordered appendix tables (Table 20 appears before Tables 18-19 that are discussed first).

Comparison fairness: latency-normalized comparisons mix locally profiled open models with API-based closed models on different hardware and pricing assumptions, and the 'GPT-5.2' rows are meaningless given that model does not exist.

strengths: Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art execution accuracy on BIRD-dev (77.84%) and Spider-test (89.75%) trained only on BIRD, with strong out-of-domain transfer (SParC, Spider-DK).

Unusually thorough ablation and attribution analysis: component ablations (Table 2), dataset-wide controlled isolation (Table 3), selection-strategy comparisons (Fig. 4, Table 32), turn-budget ablations (Table 24), and Best-of-N analysis (Table 25) give a fine-grained picture of where gains come from.

The paper directly confronts the most obvious confound—parameter count—via a parameter-matched ~21B ensemble baseline (Table 18), generator scaling 7B→14B (Table 19), and single-model multi-task baselines at 14B/32B (Table 20), which strengthens the claim that role specialization, not scale, drives the gains.

Comprehensive efficiency reporting (latency, token cost, VRAM under different deployment assumptions, normalized time budgets, tunable cost-accuracy operating points) that is rare and valuable for agentic systems papers.

Honest treatment of limitations: the conclusion explicitly discusses the ~21B footprint and the specialization-vs-scaling trade-off rather than hiding it; training details, prompts, and dataset construction are documented in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core ingredients (GRPO with sparse execution rewards, ReAct-style multi-turn tool use, generative verifiers as next-token prediction, grounding/generation/validation decomposition) are each established; the closest prior work, SkyRL-SQL (Liu et al., 2025b, cited by the authors), already does multi-turn RL for Text-to-SQL with execution feedback. The conclusion's claim of being 'the first framework to leverage an interactive RL policy for tool-augmented SQL generation' is overclaimed relative to this prior work.

Validation Agent training data has circularity concerns: verifier pairs are built from trajectories generated by the same generator being evaluated, and for questions with no correct candidates the authors inject the ground-truth SQL into prompts to force trajectory generation (Appendix C.1). This creates a train-time distribution that differs from test time and raises questions about how much of the verifier's near-oracle selection performance (89.75% selected vs. 90.68% Pass@8 on Spider-test, i.e., within one point of the oracle) reflects genuine verification skill versus distribution artifacts.

Citation and reporting integrity issues that undermine trust: references include impossible future arXiv identifiers (e.g., arXiv:2601.03267 for a 'GPT-5 system card', arXiv:2605.01357 dated 2026), a 'GPT-5.2' model in Tables 13–14 that is not clearly specified, and the abstract's 'Code is available at' is followed by an empty link. These suggest rushed or unverifiable sourcing for headline baselines.

The data-efficiency claim (matching MARS-SQL would require 'approximately 15 million synthetic examples and 3–4 months of training') is a speculative scaling-law extrapolation, not an experiment, and should not be presented as evidence of orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains.

No variance reporting: results appear to be single runs without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite headline improvements of a few points over strong baselines on a 1,534-example dev set.

Some internal inconsistencies: Figure 6's example trajectory shows thoughts/observations out of order relative to the rounds described, and 'detaile in Appendix E' and similar typos persist; small but they reduce confidence in carefulness of the writeup.

Baseline comparability is imperfect: closed-source agentic systems (CHESS, XiYan-SQL, CHASE-SQL) use much stronger backbone models, and the most competitive open-source competitor on Spider-DK (Arctic-Text2SQL-R1, 81.5%) trained on Spider itself, so the 'state-of-the-art' framing requires careful reading, which the paper mostly but not always provides.
